narration: Here's something wild. Your mutual fund lost eighteen percent last year — and the IRS still sent you a $1,842 tax bill. It's called phantom income, and it's been quietly hitting your account for years.
visual: IRS tax notice document with $1,842 amount due, overlaid on a small downward stock chart line

narration: Here's how it works. When your fund manager sells winning stocks inside the fund, those gains flow to every investor — including you. You didn't sell a single share, but you still owe the taxes.
visual: Fund manager person at top distributing dollar-sign arrows to three investor silhouettes below

narration: In 2022, the market crashed eighteen percent. But fund companies still distributed one point three trillion dollars in capital gains. Investors were losing money and getting IRS bills at the exact same time.
visual: Stock chart line dropping sharply left to right, IRS tax notice document appearing over the low point

narration: It gets worse. That tax bill is real cash out of your pocket even if you reinvest the distribution. You lose on the fund drop, then pay taxes on gains you didn't choose to take. Two hits, zero wins.
visual: Person silhouette in center with two red arrows draining outward — left labeled LOSS, right labeled TAX, coins falling from both

narration: Number one fix — use ETFs in your taxable accounts. Eighty percent of active mutual funds distribute capital gains every single year. ETFs? Near zero. Same market exposure, dramatically less phantom tax.
visual: Side-by-side cards: ETF card with green checkmark and NEAR 0% DISTRIBUTIONS vs MUTUAL FUND card with red X and 80% DISTRIBUTE

narration: Pull up your 1099-DIV from last year. If box 2a has a number, that's phantom income you paid taxes on. Switch your taxable accounts to low-cost ETFs and stop paying for money you never actually received.
visual: 1099-DIV tax form with box 2a highlighted in red showing $1,842, then rising ETF trend line and follow CTA
